medium.titulo: 5 AI Automations Every Content Creator Should Build in 2026
medium.resumo: Creating content is only half the job. The other half is everything around it: writing captions, posting on several platforms, replying to…
medium.conteudo_html:
Creating content is only half the job. The other half is everything around it: writing captions, posting on several platforms, replying to comments, researching ideas and tracking results. For most creators, this “invisible work” takes more time than making the content itself.

The good news is that much of it can now be automated. With a workflow tool like n8n and an AI model such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini, you can build small systems that handle the boring parts while you focus on creating.

This expanded guide does three things the short version did not: it explains in detail what AI automation actually is, it goes deep on each of the five automations with step-by-step setups, and it adds five AI tools that make all of it possible. Read it once, pick one automation, and build it this week.

Part 1: What Is AI Automation, Really?

AI automation = a boring, repeated task + an AI that can think through it + a tool that runs it for you, automatically.

Traditional automation follows fixed rules: “if this happens, do that.” It is fast but dumb — it cannot handle anything unexpected. AI automation adds a brain to the system. The AI reads, understands, decides and writes, so the workflow can handle messy, real-world work like writing a caption in your tone or deciding whether a comment is a question or spam.

Every AI automation has three parts

1. A trigger — something starts the work.

A new YouTube video is published. A comment arrives. It is Monday at 9 a.m. A link is sent to a chatbot. The trigger is the “when”.

2. An AI brain — the thinking step.

An AI model like Claude or ChatGPT reads the input and does the thinking: summarise this video, write a caption for LinkedIn, sort these comments, suggest ten ideas. This is the step old automation could never do.

3. An action — something happens.

The caption is posted. The summary arrives in your chat. The ideas land in a Google Sheet. The reply draft waits for your review. The action is the “what happens next”.

Trigger → AI brain → Action. That is the whole pattern. Every automation in this article follows it.

Automation vs AI automation A real example, end to end

You publish a YouTube video at 6 p.m. Within two minutes, without you touching anything:

1. The workflow sees the new video (trigger).

2. Claude reads the title and description and writes three captions — professional for LinkedIn, casual for Facebook, short for X (AI brain).

3. Each caption is posted to the right platform (action).

You did nothing. Your audience on three platforms saw your video within minutes.

What AI automation cannot do

Be honest about the limits, or the system will disappoint you:

· It cannot be you. AI can copy your style, but it cannot have your opinions, stories or judgement. Always review before publishing.

· It cannot check facts. AI can invent numbers, quotes and news. Verify anything factual before it goes out.

· It cannot build trust alone. Audiences follow people, not workflows. Automation should give you more time with your audience, not replace you.

Part 2: The 5 Automations, In Detail

1. Auto-Post New Content to Every Platform

The problem: You publish a YouTube video or blog post, then spend 20 minutes sharing it on LinkedIn, Facebook, X and other platforms, each with a different caption. Most creators skip platforms simply because sharing takes too long — and lose the audience there.

How it works, step by step:

Trigger: An RSS feed node watches your YouTube channel or blog. When something new appears, the workflow starts.

AI brain: The title and description go to Claude or ChatGPT with a clear prompt: “Write a LinkedIn caption (professional, 150 words, end with a question), a Facebook caption (casual, friendly), and an X post (under 280 characters). Keep my tone: simple, direct, helpful.”

Action: The workflow posts each caption to the right platform automatically — or saves them as drafts if you prefer to review first.

Tools you need: n8n (free self-hosted or cloud trial), a YouTube RSS feed, Claude or ChatGPT API, and the posting nodes for each platform. SolMarrow (free) can also schedule the posts if you prefer drafts over instant posting.

Time it saves: roughly 20 minutes per post. Posting three times a week, that is about 4 hours a month — back in your pocket.

2. Summarise Videos and Articles in Seconds

The problem: Staying updated in your niche means watching long videos and reading long articles every day. Nobody has time for all of it — so most creators slowly fall behind on trends.

How it works, step by step:

Trigger: You send a YouTube link or article link to a chatbot on Telegram or WhatsApp.

AI brain: The workflow fetches the transcript or article text and asks AI for a short summary: five key points, one surprising idea, and one content idea it sparks.

Action: The summary arrives back in your chat within seconds.

Tools you need: n8n, a Telegram bot (free), a YouTube transcript tool, Claude or ChatGPT API.

Time it saves: a 20-minute video becomes a 30-second read. Following ten sources a day stops being impossible.

Pro tip: Ask the AI for “one content idea this sparks” every time. Your research feed becomes an idea machine as well.

3. Generate Content Ideas Every Week

The problem: Creative block. Every creator knows the feeling of staring at a blank page on Monday morning, with a week of posting ahead.

How it works, step by step:

1. Trigger: A schedule node runs every Monday at 9 a.m.

2. AI brain: The workflow collects trending headlines from news sites or RSS feeds in your niche, sends them to AI, and asks for ten content ideas — each with a suggested title and a first-line hook.

3. Action: The list arrives in your email or a Google Sheet, ready for the week.

Tools you need: n8n, RSS feeds in your niche, Claude or ChatGPT API, Google Sheets or email.

Time it saves: the blank-page hour disappears. You start Monday choosing from ten ideas instead of searching for one.

Pro tip: Feed the AI your last ten best-performing posts as well, and ask for “more ideas like these”. The ideas get sharper because they are built on what your audience already liked.

4. Turn One Piece of Content into Many

The problem: You spend hours making one long video or article, but it only gets used once. Meanwhile the creators who post daily are not working five times harder — they are reusing one piece of work five times.

How it works, step by step:

4. Trigger: You drop a video transcript or article text into a folder or a form.

5. AI brain: AI repurposes it into a LinkedIn post, a Twitter/X thread, a short newsletter, five quote cards and two short video scripts — each in your tone.

6. Action: The results are saved in Google Docs or Notion for your review, ready to schedule through the week.

Tools you need: n8n, Claude or ChatGPT API, Google Docs or Notion, and Opus Clip for turning long videos into short clips automatically.

Time it saves: one hour of recording becomes a full week of posts. This is the single highest-leverage automation on this list.

Pro tip: Repurpose within 24 hours of publishing, while the topic is fresh. A week-old video repurposed late feels stale; the same content reused the next day feels like a series.

5. Manage Comments and Messages

The problem: As your audience grows, comments and messages pile up, and important ones get lost — a collaboration offer buried under spam, a genuine question never answered.

How it works, step by step:

7. Trigger: New comments and messages are collected from your platforms into one workflow.

8. AI brain: AI sorts them into categories: questions, praise, collaboration requests and spam. It drafts polite replies to common questions and flags business enquiries instantly.

9. Action: You get one tidy digest — questions to answer, praise to like, business messages to prioritise, spam already filtered out.

Tools you need: n8n, the comment APIs or integrations of your platforms, Claude or ChatGPT API.

Time it saves: instead of opening four apps and scrolling, you handle everything from one list in minutes.

Pro tip: Always review AI-drafted replies before sending. Your audience wants to hear from you, not a robot. Use AI to draft, never to send, on this one.

Part 3: 5 AI Tools Every Content Creator Should Know

These are the tools behind the five automations above. Each one is useful on its own — together, they are a complete creator system. All five have a free way to start.

1. n8n — the automation hub (free to self-host)
How it works: n8n connects your apps and AI together into visual workflows. It is the engine that runs all five automations in this article — the triggers, the AI steps and the posting actions all live here.
Cost: free if you self-host it on your own computer or a small server; n8n Cloud has a free trial, then paid plans.
Best for: creators who want full control and zero monthly fees. If you can only learn one tool from this list, learn this one.
How it fits: it is the backbone. Automations 1–5 all run on it.

2. Claude (or ChatGPT) — the AI brain (free tier available)
What it does: the thinking step. Claude and ChatGPT read, summarise, write captions, sort comments and generate ideas. Claude is especially strong at long text and keeping a consistent tone; ChatGPT is strong at breadth and integrations. Pick one and learn its style.
Cost: both have free tiers; API use is pay-as-you-go and costs only cents per workflow run for typical creator tasks.
Best for: every writing and thinking step in the five automations.
How it fits: it is the “AI brain” in every workflow. The quality of your prompts decides the quality of your output — write prompts that describe your tone, your audience and the exact format you want.
3. Descript — edit video and audio by editing text (free plan available)
What it does: Descript turns your video or podcast into a transcript, and you edit the media by editing the words — delete a sentence from the text and it disappears from the video. It also removes filler words (“um”, “uh”) in one click and can clone your voice for small corrections.
Cost: free plan with limited hours; paid plans for regular creators.
Best for: creators who record long videos or podcasts and hate traditional timeline editing. It is also the fastest way to get a clean transcript for Automation 4 (repurposing).
How it fits: record once, get a transcript in minutes, feed it to Automation 4, and one recording becomes a week of content.

4. Opus Clip — turn long videos into viral shorts (free trial)

What it does: Opus Clip watches a long video, finds the most engaging moments, and cuts them into vertical short clips with captions and a virality score for each clip. What takes an hour by hand takes minutes.
Cost: free trial with limited clips; paid plans for regular use.
Best for: YouTubers and anyone with long videos who wants Reels, Shorts and TikToks without extra filming.
How it fits: it is the video half of Automation 4. Your long video becomes five shorts, and each short links back to the full video.

5. SolMarrow — schedule posts to every platform, free forever
What it does: SolMarrow is a free social media scheduler — connect LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram and more, write once, and schedule posts to all of them. No card required, unlimited posts on the free plan, and it works with n8n so your automations can schedule instead of posting instantly.
Cost: free forever.
Best for: creators who want their auto-generated captions reviewed and scheduled — not blasted out instantly — and who do not want another monthly subscription.
How it fits: it is the safe “action” step for Automation 1 and Automation 4. The AI writes, you review, SolMarrow schedules.

The system, in one line
n8n runs it, Claude thinks it, Descript and Opus Clip multiply it, SolMarrow schedules it.
How to Get Started
Always Caution !!
Automation should support your creativity, not replace it. Keep these points in mind:
• Keep your voice. Edit AI output so it sounds like you. If your audience cannot tell the difference, you have gone too far.
• Check facts. AI can make mistakes, especially with numbers and news. Verify before publishing.
• Follow platform rules. Some platforms limit automated posting. Drafts and scheduling are safer than instant auto-posting.
• Protect your accounts. Keep API keys and passwords private. Never paste them into a chat or a shared document.
• Review replies yourself. Automation 5 drafts replies — you send them.
Conclusion
The creators who grow fastest are not always the most talented; they are often the most consistent. AI automation gives you that consistency by handling the repetitive work, so your energy goes into what only you can do: creating.
Start with one automation this week. Once you see the time it saves, you will want to build the other four. And once the five are running, add the five tools — that combination is a complete content system, built for free or nearly free.
Which of these five automations would help you most? Tell me in the comments.

medium.conteudo_html:
I think my idea about super-fast memory needs describing in more detail. Before that, it would be worth running some deep research on whether I am the inventor of this idea or not.

Here is how it works for me.

I start a session. Say I have arrived at Web Summit and want to do something there. I do not want the session going off to Luma from scratch, checking things and so on. I want the session to look first at what has already been done on this subject by other sessions, and only then go and verify it against external sources.

So the session searches sessions first. It starts doing recall. Every time a session does something, it looks at whether something has already been done on this topic — even if I did not explicitly ask.

Then it recalls: it can search the freshest memory, the top layer, the last few weeks. And it finds a pile of sessions that already did this work for it.

So it says: I looked through the sessions, and today’s events are these. However, looking through the sessions, I also learned that you recently asked about a hurricane. And there is indeed a hurricane today.

Since we all want our co-founder to be proactive, it additionally went and searched the internet. On the internet it turns out there is indeed a hurricane today. And since there is a hurricane, it occurred to it that some meetups might be cancelled. So it went and re-checked Luma, and some meetups had indeed been cancelled.

After that it hands back a list of meetups based on two things: it searched past sessions, and it verified the information against real sources. And it concludes: these are the places you should go.

Very important. First: the system acts on its own. Second: the system searches the most recent sessions. Because if we have already burned a fortune in tokens on this question, why discuss it all over again every time?

Plus, if Mycroft understands that something could have changed, it will go and check and re-verify. If we know the data can change — flight schedules, meetups, meetings — then it is very important to look at whether it has. Same with the weather.

In short, it is very important always to use two layers of memory. If the top layer turns up nothing, we dig deeper.

And here is the important bit: I do not know how to make Mycroft understand by itself whether it is worth searching deeper or not. Web Summit is events. Events are planned for today, and they were unlikely to be discussed six months ago — though they might have been. So we should always search the top layer. But if searching the old memory is not very expensive, we could search there too.

At the same time one has to understand: is that old memory needed at all? Or is it useless because it has gone stale?

That is a very good question. I do not know the right way to handle it. How would you advise doing it? Because honestly, I do not know.

I went and checked. Both answers already exist, and one of them is mine from two months ago.

First, the prior art, since I asked whether I invented this

I did not.

| system | memory model | what it does with stale facts |
| — -| — -| — -|
| Zep / Graphiti | temporal knowledge graph, explicitly bi-temporal: when the event happened, and when it was ingested | marks facts superseded rather than burying them |
| Letta | context window as an operating system: in-context, core, archival tiers | the agent self-edits its own memory |
| Mem0 | a layer between model and app over vector, graph and key-value stores | add / update / delete, replacing stale entries |

Zep publishes 94.8% on Deep Memory Retrieval against 93.4% for MemGPT — their own benchmark, not an independent one. And the general advice in the field has already hardened into a slogan: invalidate, do not discard, so that past states stay reconstructible.

So the two layers are not mine, the bi-temporal axis is not mine, and the tiering is not mine.

What I could not find in any of the three is the thing I mentioned almost in passing in my own post: the chain. Recall first, then judge whether the world may have moved, then verify externally, then hand back a merged answer — unprompted. All three store and retrieve beautifully. None of them re-checks a venue listing because a hurricane might have cancelled something.

That is the part worth describing in more detail. Not the layers.

Second, the question I asked the room was measured on 16 September

The engine exists. It holds note facts on two axes — when a thing is true in the world, and when we observed it — plus whether the source was a machine or a human. Deliberately the same columns as the memory layer next to it, so two implementations of one time model cannot quietly drift apart.

And it carries a rule with a count behind it:

> A filter showing only currently-valid material is forbidden. Measured on a frozen test set: of 184 questions, three had a correct answer that was itself closed — superseded notes. Filtering by freshness would have zeroed those three by construction.

So the answer to “is the old memory needed, or is it stale and useless” is: do not decide. Rank. Push closed material down instead of out, because sometimes the right answer lives in the note that was retired.

Which is the same conclusion the field reached independently, with the difference that ours came with three counted failures attached.

And one correction about my own system

I described two layers as if they were one store with a freshness filter on top. They are not. They are two separate indexes, on purpose:

| index | contents | job |
| — -| — -| — -|
| curated essence | distilled notes, decisions, insights | the sharp recall |
| Chat Book | exported session transcripts, human sessions only | find which past conversation covered a topic |

The reason is written into the engine itself: raw chat chatter must never pollute the curated mind. Service and robot chats are filtered out before indexing. The two share an embedding model but hold separate locks so both can rebuild at the same time.

Which sharpens my own design question. It is not “recent or old” by age. It is episodic or semantic by kind — did this happen in a conversation, or is it a distilled fact — with age as a ranking signal inside each. I had been asking the wrong question, which is why it felt unanswerable.

The best comment under the post is almost a description of that

Somebody proposed a StackOverflow for agents: a retrieval layer over problem summaries and their solutions, votes on the solutions, exposed as an MCP with search over solved cases and filters so sensitive data cannot leak. Their hypothesis: search saves tokens.

And then the line that is sharper than anything in my own post: the question is not so much how to build it, but how to prove the value and earn from it.

They are describing the Chat Book plus two things I do not have — votes on solutions, and a surface other people’s agents can call. The leak filter they worry about is partly handled on my side by excluding service and robot sessions, but it becomes a prerequisite rather than a feature the moment anybody else can query it.

What I take from this

Three things.

I asked the room a question I had already answered with a measurement, two months earlier, on my own machines. That is the second time this week I have published a feature request for something I own, and the cause is not forgetfulness — it is that the system is now larger than my memory of it, which is precisely the problem the system was built to solve.

The part of the idea that is actually mine is the smallest sentence in the post. Not two layers — Zep, Letta and Mem0 have tiers and a published benchmark. The recall-then-verify-then-merge chain, run without being asked, is the thing with no equivalent, and I buried it under an architecture paragraph.

And a commenter named the real gap in one line. The storage question has three vendors and a benchmark. The value question — how to prove this is worth anything, and how to earn from it — has nobody, including me.

⚠️ Caveats. The prior-art numbers are vendor self-published: both the 94.8% and the 93.4% come from Zep’s own benchmark, and I found no independent head-to-head. The engines and indexes above were read from source and from my own records rather than exercised for this piece, and the September measurement is quoted from the record of that run rather than re-run today. The temporal engine and its state live on another machine, so nothing here was re-measured locally. The three-of-184 figure is one frozen test set at one moment, which is enough to forbid a filter and not enough to size a ranking. And “search saves tokens” is a hypothesis on both sides — the commenter’s and mine — until somebody actually counts the tokens.

import { useLocalStorage } from "@vueuse/core";

export type CartItem = {
  id: string;
  slug: string;
  title: string;
  price: number;
  image_url: string | null;
  stock: number;
  qty: number;
};

export type CartProduct = Omit<CartItem, "qty">;

export const useCart = () => {
  // initOnMounted: server dan render pertama client sama-sama kosong, jadi tidak ada hydration mismatch
  const items = useLocalStorage<CartItem[]>("resto-cart", [], {
    initOnMounted: true,
  });

  const count = computed(() => items.value.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0));
  const total = computed(() =>
    items.value.reduce((n, i) => n + i.price * i.qty, 0),
  );

  const qtyOf = (id: string) => items.value.find((i) => i.id === id)?.qty ?? 0;

  /** true = berhasil ditambah, false = stok habis atau sudah mencapai batas stok */
  function add(product: CartProduct) {
    if (product.stock <= 0) return false;

    const existing = items.value.find((i) => i.id === product.id);
    if (existing) {
      // segarkan data dari server supaya harga dan stok tidak basi
      existing.price = product.price;
      existing.stock = product.stock;
      if (existing.qty >= product.stock) return false;
      existing.qty++;
    } else {
      items.value.push({ ...product, qty: 1 });
    }
    return true;
  }

  function setQty(id: string, qty: number) {
    const item = items.value.find((i) => i.id === id);
    if (!item) return;
    item.qty = Math.max(1, Math.min(qty, item.stock));
  }

  function remove(id: string) {
    items.value = items.value.filter((i) => i.id !== id);
  }

  function clear() {
    items.value = [];
  }

  return { items, count, total, qtyOf, add, setQty, remove, clear };
};

-- Buat pesanan: cek stok, kurangi stok, simpan item, hitung total. Satu transaksi.
create or replace function public.create_order(
  p_user_id uuid, p_client_key uuid, p_order_type text, p_table_number text,
  p_customer_name text, p_phone text, p_note text, p_payment_method text, p_items jsonb
) returns uuid
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = public
as $$
declare
  v_order_id uuid;
  v_total bigint := 0;
  v_item record;
  v_product record;
begin
  -- klik ganda atau retry: kembalikan pesanan yang sama
  select id into v_order_id from orders
  where client_key = p_client_key and user_id = p_user_id;
  if v_order_id is not null then return v_order_id; end if;

  if jsonb_typeof(p_items) <> 'array'
     or jsonb_array_length(p_items) not between 1 and 30 then
    raise exception 'INVALID_ITEMS';
  end if;

  insert into orders (user_id, client_key, order_type, table_number, customer_name,
                      phone, note, payment_method)
  values (p_user_id, p_client_key, p_order_type, p_table_number, p_customer_name,
          p_phone, p_note, p_payment_method)
  returning id into v_order_id;

  -- diurutkan: urutan kunci baris konsisten, mencegah deadlock antar pesanan
  for v_item in
    select (e ->> 'product_id')::uuid as product_id, sum((e ->> 'qty')::int)::int as qty
    from jsonb_array_elements(p_items) e
    group by 1
    order by 1
  loop
    if v_item.qty < 1 or v_item.qty > 50 then
      raise exception 'INVALID_QTY';
    end if;

    select id, title, price, stock into v_product
    from products where id = v_item.product_id for update;

    if not found then
      raise exception 'PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND';
    end if;
    if v_product.stock < v_item.qty then
      raise exception 'OUT_OF_STOCK:%', v_product.title;
    end if;

    update products set stock = stock - v_item.qty where id = v_product.id;

    insert into order_items (order_id, product_id, title, price, qty)
    values (v_order_id, v_product.id, v_product.title, v_product.price, v_item.qty);

import type { H3Event } from "h3";
import {
  serverSupabaseUser,
  serverSupabaseServiceRole,
} from "#supabase/server";

export async function requireUser(event: H3Event) {
  const claims = await serverSupabaseUser(event);
  const userId = claims?.sub;

import { serverSupabaseClient } from "#supabase/server";

const schema = z.object({ ids: z.array(z.string().uuid()).min(1).max(30) });

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const parsed = schema.safeParse(await readBody(event));
  if (!parsed.success) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 400, statusMessage: "Invalid input" });
  }

  const client = await serverSupabaseClient(event);
  const { data, error } = await client
    .from("products")
    .select("id, title, price, stock")

      statusCode: 500,
      statusMessage: "Gagal memuat keranjang",
    });
  }

medium.titulo: Why I stopped choosing a component library for each framework
medium.resumo: So I built VinUI: one free set of UI components, eight visual styles, and the same markup in HTML, React, Vue and Svelte.
medium.conteudo_html:
So I built VinUI: one free set of UI components, eight visual styles, and the same markup in HTML, React, Vue and Svelte.

I write a lot of small web projects. Some are plain HTML pages, some are React apps, and lately a few are in Vue and Svelte. For years, each new project started with the same question: which component library this time?

The answer was never satisfying. The good libraries were tied to one framework, so my HTML landing page and my Vue app ended up using two libraries that looked nothing alike. And most libraries had exactly one personality. You could swap the brand colour, but the result still looked like every other site built with the same kit.

So I tried something different, and this week I launched it: VinUI, a free, MIT-licensed component library. It’s live on Product Hunt today.

The idea: one component, one API, four frameworks

Every VinUI component starts as a single API spec. The plain-HTML version is checked against that spec, and the React, Vue and Svelte versions are tested to render exactly the same markup as the HTML.

That sounds like a small detail, but it changes a lot. If the markup is identical, the styling is identical, the accessibility behaviour is identical, and even the screenshots are identical. The only thing that changes between frameworks is the syntax you write.

Here is a button in plain HTML:

<button class="vin-btn vin-btn--outline">Save</button>

And the same button in React, Vue or Svelte:

<Button variant="outline">Save</Button>

Both produce the same element on the page.

Eight styles instead of one look

The second problem was personality. Instead of one theme with a colour picker, VinUI has eight complete visual styles. Each one is a set of design tokens, and the CSS is generated from them, so every component reads the same token names in every style:

  • Precision: crisp hairlines, for dev tools and SaaS
  • Tactile: physical, pressable buttons, for productivity apps
  • Clay: puffy and friendly, for onboarding and education
  • Tonal: colour-led pill shapes, for consumer apps
  • Editorial: typographic and airy, for blogs and portfolios
  • Terminal: monospace and developer-native, for CLI docs
  • Paper: warm and hand-made, for personal sites
  • Bento: calm, layered and borderless, for product sites

Each style works with any accent colour, in light and dark mode. The whole theme is set on one element:

<html data-vin-style="tactile" data-vin-mode="dark" style="--vin-accent: #0d9488">

Change one attribute and the entire interface follows. On the VinUI site you can try this live: pick a style in the header and the whole site restyles itself.

You own the code

I didn’t want another dependency to keep updated. VinUI has a small CLI that copies the component source straight into your project:

npx @vinish/ui init
npx @vinish/ui add button

It reads your framework from package.json, writes the files, and records them in a vin.json file. From then on the code is yours to change. When I ship an update, npx @vinish/ui diff shows what changed, and your own edits are kept.

It doesn’t need Tailwind or any other CSS framework either. VinUI ships its own small CSS files, and it can sit alongside Tailwind if your project already uses it.

Accessibility wasn’t optional

Every component has keyboard support, focus handling and ARIA attributes, and is checked against WCAG 2.2 AA in all eight styles, in both light and dark mode. Automated tests take screenshots and run accessibility checks across every combination.

I also wanted the plain-HTML version to degrade gracefully. Only components with keyboard or pointer behaviour need the one small script, and it has no dependencies. Dialogs use the browser’s native dialog element. Without JavaScript, the carousel still swipes, the charts still draw and the data table still shows its first page.

What’s in the box

  • 63 components, from buttons and inputs to a combobox, date picker, data table, command menu and sidebar
  • 7 AI chat components (messages, bubbles, attachments, traces and more) for anyone building a chat interface
  • 13 blocks: ready-made sections such as sign-in, a dashboard, settings, pricing, FAQ, contact and a 404 page
  • 16 charts in plain SVG, with tooltips, keyboard support and a data table for screen readers, and no chart library

It works with AI coding assistants too

Because adding a component is a single command, tools like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Copilot can run it the same way you do. They get real components in your framework and your chosen style, instead of inventing markup. There’s also an llms.txt file on the site that describes the library for language models.

Try it

VinUI is free and open source under the MIT license.

  • Docs and live demo: vinish.dev/ui
  • Source code: github.com/devvinish/vin-ui
  • Product Hunt: producthunt.com/posts/vinui

If it looks useful, an upvote or comment on Product Hunt today would mean a lot. And I’d genuinely like to hear which of the eight styles you’d pick, and which component you’d want me to build next.

corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quinta-feira | 26 de novembro de 2026

Um problemão para as corridas de rua está em discussão em Salvador, na Bahia. O vereador João Cláudio Bacelar (Podemos) apresentou um Projeto de Lei (nº 319/2026) na Câmara Municipal que visa proibir o uso de som alto, como música e locução, antes das 7h da manhã nos dias de provas. A proposta surge em resposta a reclamações de moradores de diversos bairros, que relatam que o barulho das corridas e caminhadas começa por volta das 5h da manhã, atrapalhando o descanso.

O projeto não proíbe a realização das corridas antes das 7h, mas veta o uso de qualquer tipo de amplificação sonora, música ou locução que desrespeitem os limites e horários da lei do som urbano da capital. O texto também sugere que, preferencialmente, esses eventos sejam autorizados em locais não residenciais ou de menor impacto para a vizinhança. A questão é delicada: por um lado, os corredores querem largar cedo para aproveitar temperaturas mais amenas; por outro, há o direito ao descanso dos moradores. É um debate que precisa ser feito com bom senso e respeito por todas as partes.

Corrida Integração de Campinas agora terá maratona

Foi lançada oficialmente a nova fase da Corrida Integração de Campinas, que em 2027 passará a contar com uma maratona de 42 km. Em um evento realizado na última quarta-feira, Caio Maciel, diretor de marketing do grupo que organiza a prova, confirmou que a maratona terá um percurso de volta única, uma demanda antiga da comunidade de corrida. A organização já trabalha há dois anos na negociação com o poder público para viabilizar o trajeto, que ainda passará por aprovações finais antes de ser divulgado.

A prova, considerada a “São Silvestre do interior”, busca elevar seu padrão e já pleiteia o selo Ouro da World Athletics. Além da maratona, o evento manterá as distâncias de 5 km, 10 km, 21 km e a caminhada. Outra novidade é o “Desafio 5 e 42”, para quem quiser encarar as duas distâncias. Para apoiar o evento, foi criada uma plataforma de conteúdo dentro do portal GE.globo chamada “Correndo”, além de um quadro fixo no Globo Esporte local e pílulas de conteúdo nas rádios do grupo. As inscrições já estão abertas com valor promocional.

Forcell lança programa para apoiar estreantes na maratona

A Forcell lançou o “Programa Primeira Maratona 2027”, uma iniciativa para apoiar corredores que vão estrear na distância dos 42,195 km. O programa selecionará oito atletas, um para cada uma das maratonas do Circuito Brasil Gigante, e oferecerá suplementação individualizada durante todo o ciclo de preparação, além de apoio nutricional e assessoria esportiva parceira opcional.

Em troca, a Forcell pede apenas que os selecionados compartilhem sua jornada de treinos de forma real e autêntica em suas redes sociais, sem roteiros ou superproduções. O objetivo é mostrar a realidade da preparação para uma maratona. Para participar, é preciso ter mais de 18 anos, já estar inscrito em uma das maratonas do circuito (ou outra, que será avaliada) e preencher o formulário no site da marca, contando sua história e por que merece ser escolhido. As maratonas do Circuito Brasil Gigante são: Paraná, São Paulo, Porto Alegre, Campo Grande, João Pessoa, Florianópolis, Salvador e Aracaju. As inscrições podem ser feitas pelo site Forcell Performance.
